prize_parts.citation: for precision measurements of the anisotropies of the cosmic microwave background that established the age, geometry and composition of the universe

statement.case_for: I keep the precision CMB candidate first, and I want to be honest that it is the least supported on the table: only Mark Pearce and I ranked it at all. The reason is that it is the discovery that most directly answers to nature. WMAP and Planck turned the age, flatness and the dark-matter and dark-energy budget of the universe from a loose set of ideas into numbers at the percent level, and every theorist working on dark energy, myself included, has to live with those numbers. Nothing in the later literature has overturned them. The measurement is fully mature, independently confirmed by WMAP, Planck and ground and balloon experiments, and no earlier prize covers this era: COBE (2006) was the blackbody spectrum and the first anisotropies, and the 2019 prize to Peebles was for theoretical cosmology. As someone who announced the 2019 prize I can say that the committee deliberately left the measurement side open. A Bennett, Spergel and Puget configuration spans both satellites and covers the instrument, the analysis and the theory interpretation.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is attribution. A satellite mission has hundreds of essential contributors, the three-name limit forces us to choose between WMAP and Planck, and the credited list contains four names of which at most three can be used. Whichever trio we choose will look arbitrary to part of the community (Page versus Puget is exactly this problem). A second objection is breadth of support: if the committee finds that only two of us rank it, then the candidate may simply not be the committee's best discovery, and persistence on my part should not be mistaken for merit. The optical lattice clock (B030) has far broader support and much cleaner credit, and I would not be unhappy to see it win.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B055 third and prefers Bennett, Spergel and Page, noting that the 2006 COBE prize and the 2019 cosmology prize make novelty arguable and that a three-name limit excludes Planck leadership.
responses.response: I take the overlap point seriously but I do not think it holds. COBE established the spectrum and the existence of anisotropies, not the percent-level parameters, and the 2019 prize rewarded Peebles for theory, not the measurement. I accept the real disagreement over whom to credit. Page is the strongest instrument-side name on WMAP, while Puget is the Planck HFI lead. If the committee wants a WMAP-only prize, your trio is cleaner and I would support it. I included Puget only because I think a prize that ignores Planck would misdescribe how the precision was reached. I want expert reports to settle this and I do not claim certainty.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock first, argues that Katori and Ye form a clean two-person credit, and notes that Hall's 2005 recognition makes some members feel the field is partly honoured already.
responses.response: I agree that the credit is clean and that the physics is secure, which is why I keep B030 as my first alternative and ranked it third. On the 2005 overlap I side with you: the comb was a tool for measuring optical frequencies, while the magic-wavelength lattice clock is a distinct invention. My reservation is not about merit but about framing. The clock is an instrument whose reach into fundamental physics (constant drift, redshift at the millimetre scale) is still mostly prospective, whereas the CMB has already delivered a result about the universe. I would not block the clock, and given the breadth of support it may well be the committee's natural centre of gravity.

responses.point: Kroll ranks IceCube eighth, regards the diffuse flux as firmly established but source identification as thin, and considers the discovery probably slightly early.
responses.response: I disagree in part. I ranked IceCube second, and my concern is not with the diffuse flux, which is established through several channels, but with the astrophysical interpretation, which is not. I think a prize for the discovery of the flux and the opening of the window is defensible now, in the way the 2017 gravitational-wave prize was. But I agree with you that the credit for Halzen, Karle and Spiering needs an expert report on AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND, and that waiting for more sources would cost little. That is why I keep it as an alternative rather than my first choice.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators first and argues that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp form a natural theory-experiment trio, building on the 2016 prize without repeating it.
responses.response: I ranked it fifth and the theory-experiment pairing is attractive. My difficulty is the same as yours: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe route that Molenkamp followed, and the 3D case by Fu, Kane and Mele, Moore and Balents, and Hasan is also in play. A trio that omits the person who died and two living contributors will provoke dispute. I would like to hear from you whether you see a fair way to frame the citation around the quantum spin Hall effect alone.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a satellite-based cosmology prize with the unavoidable WMAP versus Planck and Page versus Puget allocation problem.
Whether only two members ranking B055 indicates a real gap in scientific standing or only a difference in field expertise, since most of the committee are not cosmologists.
Whether the Hubble tension and other anomalies should affect how the citation is framed, even though they do not undermine the core parameter measurements.
Whether the optical lattice clock deserves precedence because of the cleaner two-person attribution and broad support.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate. I have a professional interest in the cosmology of dark energy, but I have no institutional or collaborative connection to Bennett, Spergel, Puget or Page, and no link to any other shortlisted person.
